newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia wages data clinch case for rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Australia wages data clinch case for rate cut.

text.p: Weak Australian wages data on Thursday confirmed there were no inflationary pressures in the economy in the second quarter, clinching the case for another cut in interest rates.
Bureau of Statistics data showed average weekly earnings rose by 0.5 percent in the three months to May for an annual rate of 3.7 percent, down from 4.3 percent in the March quarter.
It was the lowest quarterly rise since August 1994 and the annual rate came in well below the 4.5 percent danger zone seen by the Reserve Bank of Australia as a threat to low inflation.
Market forecasts had centred on a 0.8 percent rise for a 4.1 percent annual rate.
Economists said the figures showed that record low inflation announced on Wednesday should be locked in for at least a year.

For most, it was more a question of when, not if, the RBA would cut interest rates again to help reduce unemployment and promote stronger economic growth. Some market analysts say the cut could come as soon as Friday.
"There doesn't seem to be anything standing in the way of another rate cut," said Michael Blythe, senior economist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia.
"With an unemployment rate of 8.5 percent it would seem to be a necessity rather than something that I would like to debate," he added.

The RBA has cut the official cash rate four times over the past year, bringing it down to 5.5 percent with four equal cuts of 50 basis points. But the cuts have so far failed to work fully through to business and consumer confidence.
Workplace Relations Minister Peter Reith welcomed the data, saying they showed wage outcomes were headed in the right direction.
Reith added: "That does not of course give anybody the green light for excessive wage claims."
The Australian dollar extended an early slide after the wages data, dipping as low as US$0.7327 from an early US$0.7363/68.
The September 10-year bond futures contract hit a new record high of 93.640 in Thursday afternoon trade, overtaking the previous peak of 93.630 set in early 1994.
Despite the rate cut talk, the share market was unnerved by the data, with some investors worried that it foreshadowed continued fragile spending.

Economists questioned by Reuters were mixed as to whether the RBA would take the first opportunity to cut rates on Friday morning or would wait until after the next batch of employment data and its next board meeting on August 5.
Rob Henderson, chief economist at Dresdner Bank, put the likelihood of a rate cut at 90 percent.
"It's a fantastic number. I think it almost certainly cements low inflation over the next 12 to 18 months in our economy," Henderson said.

"From that point of view, we've got an extremely good inflation outlook on the back of a very, very good inflation performance already, so in terms of interest rates I think it's unlikely now that the Reserve won't cut. We'd have to concede that it's a 90-percent chance I think now that they will cut."
Bruce Hockman, senior economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said a cut could come as early as Friday but the Reserve Bank often found good reasons to hold off.
"In the big scheme of things in monetary policy, a couple of weeks here or there doesn't usually make a lot of difference," Hockman said.
